title: Message Queues & Async
subtitle: Decouple producers from asynchronous work with buffering and explicit delivery semantics
objectives: Decide what work belongs in the request and what belongs behind a queue
Explain how a queue decouples producer from consumer and absorbs spikes
Reason about delivery guarantees and why consumers must be idempotent
Handle the failures: retries, poison messages, ordering, and a backlog you can't drain

lessons.title: Work the user shouldn't wait for

exercises.title: Asynchronous processing defers work beyond the request-response cycle
exercises.body: A request handler can persist a job message to a queue and return after the queue accepts it. A separate worker later consumes the message and performs the slow operation, such as calling an email provider. Response latency includes job submission; job completion occurs later.
exercises.note: Defer a task only when the response remains semantically correct before that task completes. Required request decisions must remain synchronous.

exercises.prompt: An API waits 700ms for an email provider before responding. Put email delivery behind a durable queue.
exercises.beforeStatus: API RESPONSE · approximately 780ms · request waits for email
exercises.afterStatus: API RESPONSE · approximately 80ms · email continues asynchronously
exercises.result: Slow email work left the request path
exercises.why: A durable queue lets the API acknowledge accepted work without waiting for email delivery. The product must communicate that delivery is pending, and the worker needs retry and idempotency because a queued message can be delivered more than once.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: An API waits 700ms for an email provider before responding. Put email delivery behind a durable queue. Place API, Email queue, Worker. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: User → API; API → Email queue; Email queue → Worker; Worker → Email provider. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A durable queue lets the API acknowledge accepted work without waiting for email delivery. The product must communicate that delivery is pending, and the worker needs retry and idempotency because a queued message can be delivered more than once.

exercises.prompt: A user signs up. Your handler creates the account (20ms), then sends a welcome email via a third-party API (2 seconds). How long do they stare at a spinner?
choices: Over 2 seconds — they're waiting on an email they aren't even looking at
It happens in the background automatically
exercises.why: A synchronous handler returns only after all of its calls finish. The 2-second email API therefore dominates signup latency, and an email-provider outage also makes signup fail because that dependency remains on the request path.

exercises.prompt: A message ______ lets you hand off work now and have it performed later by a separate process.
exercises.why: A message queue durably records that work is required. The request can return after enqueueing, while a separate consumer later retrieves and performs the job.

exercises.prompt: Order what happens when signup sends the welcome email asynchronously.
steps: One database transaction stores the account and a welcome-email outbox record
Server responds after that transaction commits
An outbox dispatcher publishes the durable email job to the queue
A worker picks the message up and calls the email API
exercises.why: The account and outbox record commit atomically before success, so a crash cannot leave an acknowledged account with no durable email intent. A dispatcher may publish the outbox record more than once, so the queue consumer still needs a stable delivery identity and retry-safe provider handling.

exercises.prompt: Which of these belong behind a queue? Select all.
exercises.why: Email, report generation, and video encoding can finish after the request because their results are not required to continue the interaction. Login requires the password result before the server can decide whether to authenticate, so that check must remain synchronous.

exercises.prompt: What have you given up by moving the email to a queue?
choices: Certainty at response time: you told the user 'done' when the email is merely scheduled, so if it later fails, they've already been told it worked
exercises.why: An asynchronous response confirms that the job was accepted, although execution may be delayed or may fail later. This weaker completion guarantee is suitable only when the product can tolerate delayed results and has retry, monitoring, and failure-recovery paths.

exercises.prompt: Beyond speed, what does the queue give you when the email provider goes down for an hour?
choices: Signups keep working, and the messages wait in the queue until the provider returns
The queue sends the emails itself
exercises.why: The queue durably stores accepted email jobs during the provider outage. Signup can continue after a successful enqueue because email delivery runs asynchronously. When the provider recovers, consumers drain the backlog subject to retry, rate, and capacity controls.

exercises.title: An acknowledgement-based queue can redeliver unfinished work
exercises.body: In an acknowledgement-based queue, a consumer claims a durable message and acknowledges successful processing. If the claim expires first, the message becomes eligible for redelivery. Retention limits and dead-letter policies may remove or relocate it without successful processing.
exercises.note: A queue absorbs a temporary spike only while long-run consumer throughput exceeds arrival rate. Otherwise, backlog age and depth grow continuously.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: An acknowledgement-based queue can redeliver unfinished work
exercises.why: In an acknowledgement-based queue, a consumer claims a durable message and acknowledges successful processing. If the claim expires first, the message becomes eligible for redelivery. Retention limits and dead-letter policies may remove or relocate it without successful processing. A queue absorbs a temporary spike only while long-run consumer throughput exceeds arrival rate. Otherwise, backlog age and depth grow continuously.

exercises.prompt: Build the upload path so a traffic spike waits durably and video encoding scales independently of the API.
exercises.why: The upload API places each encoding job on the durable queue, and an independently scaled worker pool claims jobs before writing encoded files. If a worker crashes before acknowledging its job, the queue can redeliver it; without duplicate-safe output handling, that recovery path can create the same encoded result twice.

exercises.prompt: Black Friday: uploads spike to 10× normal, far beyond what your video encoders can handle. With a queue in front, what happens?
choices: Uploads are accepted quickly and the queue grows; workers keep chewing through at their own pace, so the backlog absorbs the spike instead of the users feeling it
exercises.why: The queue absorbs the temporary difference between arrival rate and encoder service rate, so queue depth rises while uploads remain acceptable. The backlog drains only when later service capacity exceeds arrivals; a sustained excess rate causes unbounded growth.

exercises.prompt: Jobs arrive at 1,200/sec while workers process 1,000/sec for 10 minutes. Arrivals then fall to 800/sec while workers stay at 1,000/sec. About how many minutes will the accumulated backlog take to drain?
exercises.why: The queue grows by 200 jobs/sec for 600 seconds, accumulating 120,000 jobs. After arrivals fall, workers have 1,000 − 800 = 200 jobs/sec of spare capacity, so draining takes 120,000 ÷ 200 = 600 seconds, or 10 minutes.

exercises.prompt: How do you make the backlog drain faster?
choices: Add more consumers — they pull from the same queue independently, and that's exactly the workload that scales horizontally
exercises.why: Independent messages can be distributed across additional consumers, increasing aggregate processing rate until another dependency becomes the bottleneck. Enlarging the queue adds storage for backlog but does not increase service rate.

exercises.prompt: A worker crashes halfway through processing a message. What should the queue do?
choices: Delete the message — it was delivered
Give it to another worker, since it was never acknowledged and therefore was never completed
Retry only if the worker asks
Log an error and move on
exercises.why: The queue keeps an unacknowledged message in an in-flight state. If the acknowledgement does not arrive before the visibility timeout, the queue makes the durable message available for another consumer, preventing a worker crash from losing the job.

exercises.prompt: Does adding a queue make the overall work finish sooner?
choices: No — the same work still happens, and the total takes slightly longer with the extra hop. What changed is who waits: the user doesn't
exercises.why: Queueing removes encoding from the request's critical path but does not reduce its processing time. Waiting in the backlog can increase job completion latency even while the upload response becomes faster and burst handling improves.

exercises.title: Backlog change equals arrivals minus completions
exercises.body: When 3,000 jobs arrive each second and workers finish 2,500, the queue grows by 500 jobs every second. Matching rates stops additional growth; draining existing backlog requires completion capacity above the current arrival rate.
exercises.note: Queue depth is stored waiting time. At 3,000 jobs/sec, 60,000 queued jobs represent about 20 seconds of arrivals.

exercises.prompt: A queue receives 3,000 jobs/sec. Each worker completes 500/sec. Over two minutes, choose the *fewest* workers that stop backlog growth.
exercises.why: Five workers finish 2,500 jobs/sec, leaving 500/sec to queue—60,000 jobs after two minutes. Six workers match the 3,000/sec arrival rate, so new backlog stops growing but existing backlog does not drain.

exercises.title: A queue buffers a rate mismatch; it does not erase it
exercises.body: If 3,000 jobs arrive each second and one worker pool completes 1,800, backlog grows by 1,200 jobs every second. Assigning partitions to another pool can absorb the excess, but total consumer and downstream capacity must at least match sustained arrivals.
exercises.note: Temporary bursts may queue safely. A permanent rate deficit creates unbounded waiting and storage growth.

exercises.prompt: Jobs arrive at 3,000/sec. Worker Pool A handles 1,800/sec. Drag the *smallest* share of partitions to Pool B that prevents Pool A's backlog from growing.
exercises.why: At 40%, Pool B receives 1,200 jobs/sec and Pool A receives 1,800, exactly its capacity. Below 40%, Pool A's arrival rate exceeds completion rate and its partition backlog continues growing.

exercises.title: Acknowledgement loss makes at-least-once delivery produce duplicates
exercises.body: A queue observes message delivery and acknowledgements, not the consumer's external side effects. If a consumer completes an operation and crashes before acknowledging it, the queue redelivers the unacknowledged message. This is the duplicate path in at-least-once delivery.
exercises.note: Consumers need duplicate-safe side effects. A stable operation identifier lets a downstream store recognize a repeated request and reuse its first result.

exercises.prompt: A worker finishes the job, then crashes before sending its acknowledgement. What happens to that message?
choices: It's gone — the work was done
The queue never heard 'done', so it redelivers — and the job runs a second time
The queue detects the work completed
It goes to an error log
exercises.why: The queue observes only the missing acknowledgement, so completed-but-unacknowledged work is indistinguishable from uncompleted work. It redelivers to avoid loss, creating a duplicate because the side effect and acknowledgement are not one atomic operation.

exercises.prompt: Match each delivery guarantee to what it means.

pairs.right: Zero or one processing attempt; loss is possible
Redeliver until acknowledgement while the durable message remains retained; duplicates are possible
One committed effect inside a stated transactional boundary
At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer

exercises.why: At-most-once can lose work when acknowledgement precedes processing. At-least-once retries unacknowledged work within the broker's durability and retention contract, but a crash after the effect and before acknowledgement creates a duplicate. Exactly-once claims must name the transaction boundary in which one committed effect is enforced.

exercises.prompt: Your queue is at-least-once. Your worker charges a credit card. What must be true?
choices: The worker must be idempotent: processing the same message twice must charge the customer once
exercises.why: At-least-once delivery can invoke the charge more than once. The worker must send the same idempotency key on every attempt so the payment provider records one logical charge and returns its prior result for duplicates. A local deduplication row cannot close the crash gap when that row and the external charge are separate writes.

exercises.prompt: A stream transaction atomically consumes an input record and writes its output record, but the handler also charges a credit card through an external API. What is the exactly-once boundary?
choices: The stream input and output records; the external charge still needs an idempotency key
The transaction automatically includes the credit-card provider
Only the network packet carrying the input record
There is no meaningful exactly-once boundary anywhere
exercises.why: The stream system can commit consumption and output production in one transaction, providing exactly-once processing inside that boundary. It cannot atomically roll back an external card charge, so retries still need a stable idempotency key or the provider may charge twice.

exercises.prompt: A message fails, gets retried, fails again — forever. It's blocking the queue and filling your logs. What's it called and what's the fix?
choices: A poison message: after N attempts, move it to a dead-letter queue so it stops consuming capacity and can be inspected
exercises.why: A poison message fails deterministically, so retries consume worker capacity without changing the outcome. After a configured attempt limit, a dead-letter queue isolates the original message for inspection or repair while allowing later work to proceed.

exercises.prompt: Your worker retries a failed message immediately, in a tight loop. The downstream service is already struggling. What have you built?
choices: A hammer: your retries add load to the exact service that's failing, so the retries are now part of why it can't recover
exercises.why: Immediate retries multiply traffic to an already failing dependency and can prevent recovery; this feedback loop is a retry storm. Exponential backoff increases the delay after each failure, while jitter randomizes retry times so workers do not synchronize.

exercises.title: At-least-once delivery spends extra attempts to avoid silent loss
exercises.body: A missing acknowledgement cannot reveal whether work finished before a crash. Redelivery protects against loss, but deterministic failures can consume workers forever unless retries are bounded and poison records are quarantined.
exercises.note: Idempotency controls duplicate effects; it does not control retry traffic.

exercises.prompt: The queue has 5,000 distinct jobs/sec. Failures would redeliver 60% once; consumers handle 6,500 attempts/sec. Drag the *smallest* retry share prevented by fixing poison jobs and bounded retries.
exercises.why: One retry for 60% raises load to 8,000 attempts/sec. Preventing half of those potential retries leaves 6,500. Idempotency protects effects; quarantine and retry limits protect capacity.

exercises.title: Parallel consumers can complete ordered messages out of order
exercises.body: A queue may deliver messages in sequence while multiple consumers process them concurrently. If consumer A receives the first update and runs slowly while consumer B quickly applies the second, B can finish first and A can overwrite it later.
exercises.note: Without per-entity ordering, a stale update can overwrite newer state without producing a processing error, retry, or queue alert.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Parallel consumers can complete ordered messages out of order
exercises.why: A queue may deliver messages in sequence while multiple consumers process them concurrently. If consumer A receives the first update and runs slowly while consumer B quickly applies the second, B can finish first and A can overwrite it later. Without per-entity ordering, a stale update can overwrite newer state without producing a processing error, retry, or queue alert.

exercises.prompt: Two messages for the same user: 'update email to A', then 'update email to B'. Your five workers process them in parallel. What can happen?
choices: B can land before A, leaving the email as A — the older value wins, permanently
Both are applied, ending at B
exercises.why: Parallel consumers may complete messages in a different order from publication. If email A finishes after email B, last-write-wins storage leaves A as the final value even though B was the later command.

exercises.prompt: You need those two updates to stay in order. What's the standard approach?
choices: Use an ordered partition keyed by user and allow only one in-flight message per user, or reject stale sequence numbers
exercises.why: Keyed partitioning puts one user's messages in one broker-ordered sequence, but concurrent handling or retries can still reorder effects. Serial per-key processing or sequence-number checks preserve effect order; a slow or repeatedly failing message then blocks later work for that key, creating head-of-line blocking.

exercises.prompt: Your worker updates the database, then publishes a message. It crashes in between. What's broken?
choices: The database change happened but the message never went out, so every downstream system is permanently unaware — and there's no error anywhere
exercises.why: The database update and queue publish are a dual write: a crash between them can commit the data without emitting its event. A transactional outbox writes the data and an outbox row in one database transaction; a relay then publishes that durable row with at-least-once delivery.

exercises.prompt: Which are real costs of moving work behind a queue? Select all.
choices: Debugging spans two systems and a time gap
exercises.why: At-least-once delivery permits duplicates, parallel consumers can reorder work, and asynchronous failures occur after the original request completes. A correct queued design therefore needs idempotent consumers, explicit ordering for order-sensitive operations, retry and dead-letter policies, and monitoring. Moving work off the request path can reduce response latency.

exercises.prompt: Build the 90-second export flow after the API accepts `POST /exports` and returns `202 Accepted` with a job ID.
exercises.why: The API returns a job ID without holding a 90-second request open, the queue durably buffers the job, and a worker generates the file with independent retry handling. Recording status or notifying the user gives the job ID a place to resolve to pending, failed, or ready.

exercises.prompt: Your queue backlog is 4 million messages and workers are at max. Adding workers hits the database's write limit. What now?
choices: The bottleneck moved downstream — the queue was never the constraint, so you must shed load, batch the writes, or scale the database
exercises.why: The database write limit is now the system bottleneck, so additional consumers cannot increase completed throughput. The design must reduce database work, increase database capacity, or shed input; the four-million-message backlog is accumulated capacity debt.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of queues?
choices: They make systems faster and more reliable automatically
They take work off the user's clock and decouple systems that shouldn't fail together — and charge you in duplicates, lost ordering, delayed failures, and backlogs that hide a deficit
They're only for very large systems
They guarantee work is never lost
exercises.why: A queue durably accepts work so producers and consumers can run at different times and rates. That decoupling requires handling delayed completion, backlog growth, duplicate delivery, reordering, and failures that occur after the originating request has ended.

exercises.prompt: An image worker stores a thumbnail, crashes before acknowledgement, then receives the job again. What must the handler do?
choices: Assume redelivery means the first write failed
Generate a new filename on every attempt
Use a stable image/version identity so repeating the write is harmless
exercises.why: The missing acknowledgement makes completed work indistinguishable from unfinished work. A stable identity lets the repeated attempt detect or overwrite the same intended thumbnail safely.
